title: Unsteady Gypsum Cycling as a Driver of Cryptic Perturbations in the Ancient Carbon Cycle
content:
Abstract

Earth's sedimentary record preserves large, intermittent deposits of evaporitic gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) that invoke the possibility of rapid changes in past seawater chemistry. In particular, strong imbalances between gypsum weathering and burial may drive changes in Earth's carbon cycle because calcium is a component of both gypsum and calcite/aragonite (CaCO3). Here we use a box model of the coupled calcium-sulfur-carbon cycles to simulate gypsum cycling in the late Permian and more broadly across a range of Phanerozoic conditions. We find that large gypsum weathering or burial events can produce long-lived (∼107 year) excursions in seawater alkalinity, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and pH without affecting atmospheric pCO2. For example, late Permian gypsum burial drives increases in DIC and alkalinity roughly commensurate with the effects of a permanent 50% increase in CO2 degassing, despite negligible change in pCO2. These excursions may represent a novel mechanism for generating long-lived perturbations in Earth's ancient carbon cycle; they may also be relevant to pH-based reconstructions of pCO2. The excursions documented here result from two interacting gypsum cycle drivers: tectonic forcing, which disrupts seawater carbon over <107-year timescales, and the gypsum saturation state of seawater (Ωgypsum), which stabilizes and restores the seawater carbon system toward baseline over >107-year timescales. We argue that a gypsum burial flux influenced by Ωgypsum is consistent with the Phanerozoic geochemical record and has likely stabilized the seawater carbon system since the Neoproterozoic buildup of seawater sulfate.
